# 1. Introduction

An agricultural extension officer arrives in a village with advice on when to plant, how to space a crop, and which agrochemicals to apply. Two quite different things can follow. The advice can bring a farmer within reach of a way of producing that was not previously available to them, or it can help a farmer come closer to the best they could already have achieved with the land, seed and labour they had. The first is a change in the technology a farmer can reach. The second is a change in how fully the technology already available is used. The two call for different interventions and carry different costs, and a comparison of output between served and unserved communities cannot tell them apart. Agricultural extension is nonetheless a standing recurrent commitment in most sub-Saharan African budgets, and it is judged largely on that comparison. The distinction matters most precisely where the two effects run in opposite directions. If provision improves how well farmers use what is available while the communities receiving it begin from a lower technological base, a single productivity comparison can return almost nothing while both effects are large.

The empirical literature on smallholder productivity has a well-established way of drawing this distinction. Where two groups of farmers plausibly operate different technologies, a separate production frontier can be fitted to each and both enveloped by a common meta-frontier, so that the technology a group can reach is separated from the efficiency with which its members use it [@Battese2004; @ODonnell2008]. In Ghana that machinery has been applied repeatedly to attributes of the farmer and the farm, producing a detailed picture of how technology access and efficiency vary with crop system and location [@Tsiboe2019; @Tsiboe2021; @Tsiboe2021b; @Tsiboe2022; @Ansah2023], with the age of the operator [@Asravor2024], and with gender [@Adaku2022]. Agricultural service delivery has not been examined in the same way. Where extension appears in this work it enters as a covariate in the inefficiency function, which is to say as something shifting how well a given technology is used, rather than as the boundary determining which technology is available in the first place. That is a substantive omission rather than a matter of framing, because an advisory service is precisely the kind of institution that might plausibly do either.

Ghana offers a well-suited setting for the distinction, and the reason is visible in how its services are delivered. [[CITE: one to three sentences on the institutional arrangement, to be inserted here once the source exists. This is the only assertion in the section that rests on external literature the bibliography does not yet hold, and Section 3 needs the same source for its second paragraph. Do not write the sentence around a citation that does not exist.]] The surveys used here describe a service environment with three features that bear directly on the question. Provision is close to a public monopoly: the Ministry is the provider in `r tbl_pct("table2", "share/Pooled", "v1", 1)` of farmer-communities, while non-governmental organisations reach `r tbl_pct("table2", "share/Pooled", "v2", 1)` and cooperatives `r tbl_pct("table2", "share/Pooled", "v3", 1)`. Access is contact-based rather than infrastructural: communities where an officer visits and nothing else is present account for `r tbl_pct("table3", "share/Pooled", "v3", 0)` of farmers, against `r tbl_pct("table3", "share/Pooled", "v2", 0)` where an office exists but no officer visits and `r tbl_pct("table3", "share/Pooled", "v1", 0)` where an officer is stationed but does not. And the menu is agronomically narrow: planting and seed-use advice reaches `r tbl_pct("table4", "share/Pooled", "v1", 0)` of farmer-communities and agrochemical advice `r tbl_pct("table4", "share/Pooled", "v2", 0)`, against `r tbl_pct("table4", "share/Pooled", "v6", 0)` for credit, `r tbl_pct("table4", "share/Pooled", "v7", 0)` for mechanization and `r tbl_pct("table4", "share/Pooled", "v4", 0)` for irrigation. A service consisting overwhelmingly of advice on how to use inputs a farmer already has is more plausibly an intervention in efficiency than in technology. Whether provision in fact operates through the technology available to farmers or through the efficiency with which they use it is the question this paper takes up.

We address three questions. First, do farmers in communities with an agricultural service source operate on a different production technology from otherwise comparable farmers in communities without one? Second, where a difference in overall performance appears, does it arise from the technology available to the group, from the efficiency with which that technology is used, or from both? Third, do these relationships depend on who provides the service, on what the service contains, and on when it is observed? An answer takes the form of a sign and a magnitude on each of two components rather than a single number on their product, and three measures are reported throughout: the technology gap ratio, which describes the frontier a group can reach; technical efficiency, which describes how close a farmer gets to that frontier; and meta-technical efficiency, which is their product.

To answer these questions we combine three nationally representative rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey, covering `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$prevalence$n_all), 0)` farm operators surveyed in 2005/06, 2012/13 and 2016/17, with community-level information on agricultural service provision drawn from the agriculture section of the same surveys' community questionnaire. The treatment is a property of the enumeration area rather than of the household: it records the service environment a farmer lives in, not the advice that farmer reports having received. That choice avoids the joint determination which troubles self-reported extension contact, and it carries a price we state plainly, in that it measures availability rather than uptake and so understates the difference between actual participants and non-participants. Under this definition `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$services0$GLSS5), 1)` of farmers in 2005/06 lived in a community with at least one agricultural service source, `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$services0$GLSS6), 1)` in 2012/13 and `r fmt_pct(assert_present(objs$prevalence$share$services0$GLSS7), 1)` in 2016/17. Alongside this aggregate we distinguish three institutional sources of provision, namely agricultural and fishing associations, agricultural cooperatives, and active extension delivery, and eight categories of service content.

We estimate a meta-stochastic frontier [@Battese2004; @ODonnell2008], fitting a separate translog production frontier to served and unserved communities and enveloping the two with a common meta-frontier representing the best technology available anywhere in the sample. This is what allows the technology a group can reach to be recovered separately from the efficiency with which it is used, and it is a different exercise from entering a service indicator as a regressor on a single common frontier. Because agricultural services are not randomly distributed across communities, farmers are matched one-to-one on demographic, household and production characteristics before the frontiers are estimated, and every estimate is reported on both the matched and the unmatched sample so that the contribution of matching can be read directly. Standard errors are obtained by jackknife resampling over enumeration areas. Identification rests on selection on observables, and the treatment is community availability rather than individual receipt, so what follows are associations conditional on what we observe. Section 4.4 sets out those limits in full.

The two margins run in opposite directions. Farms in served communities sit on a frontier substantially further below the meta-frontier than farms in comparable unserved communities, with a technology gap ratio of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$tgr$any), 3)` against `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$tgr$none), 3)`, a difference of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$tgr$gap), 3)`. On the same matched sample they use that frontier better, with technical efficiency of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$te$any), 3)` against `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$te$none), 3)`, a difference of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$te$gap), 3)`. Both are significant at the 1 percent level. Net of each other almost nothing remains: meta-technical efficiency differs by `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$services0$mte$gap), 3)`, roughly an order of magnitude smaller than either of the components producing it. The overall measure is therefore the least informative of the three here rather than the most. An evaluation resting on aggregate farm performance alone would have recovered a figure close to zero and concluded that agricultural service delivery makes little difference, while two large effects were present and offsetting.

Two disaggregations bear on which of the two components behaves like a consequence of the services. Across the four service types that support an estimate on the served side, the technology component barely moves, running from `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_post_harvest$provided$tgr), 3)` for post-harvest and marketing support to `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_mechanization$provided$tgr), 3)` for mechanization, while the efficiency component swings from `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_post_harvest$provided$te), 3)` to `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_service$services_mechanization$provided$te), 3)` across the same four. What a community's service menu contains bears substantially on how well farmers use the frontier available to them and very little on which frontier that is. Across survey rounds the technology gap closes, from `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_wave$tgr$gap$GLSS5), 3)` in 2005/06 to `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_wave$tgr$gap$GLSS7), 3)` in 2016/17, where it becomes the one estimate in the series not distinguishable from zero, while the efficiency difference stays positive and significant in every round. Because one component moves and the other does not, their product changes sign: overall performance in served communities sits `r fmt_num(abs(assert_present(objs$by_wave$mte$gap$GLSS5)), 3)` below unserved communities in 2005/06 and `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$by_wave$mte$gap$GLSS7), 3)` above them in 2016/17. Any single summary figure for what agricultural services did in Ghana across this period averages over a comparison that reverses direction within it.

The study contributes to the literature in three ways. First, where previous work on production shortfalls in Ghana has concentrated on attributes of the farmer and the farm, including location [@Tsiboe2019; @Tsiboe2021; @Tsiboe2021b; @Tsiboe2022; @Ansah2023], age [@Asravor2024] and gender [@Adaku2022], and where applied meta-frontier studies elsewhere have drawn the technology boundary at seed variety [@TweneboahKodua2022], production practice [@Birhanu2022] or resource endowment [@Uddin2014], we place that boundary at the institutional service environment of the community. Agricultural service delivery is treated as technology-defining rather than as a shifter of inefficiency, which is what makes the two channels separable at all. Second, where extension exposure in this literature is typically the farmer's own report of having received advice, and is therefore jointly determined with the performance being explained, we measure the service environment of the enumeration area across three nationally representative rounds spanning more than a decade; the cost, stated above, is that availability is not receipt. Third, the recurring difficulty in this work is that group membership is not randomly assigned, and the standard response has been to correct for it by matching or by an explicit selection correction [@Mayen2010; @CrespoCebada2014; @Tiedemann2013; @BravoUreta2021; @Asmare2022]. We adopt that correction and then go further, asking which of the two recovered components behaves like a consequence of the treatment and using variation in service content and across survey rounds as the test. That the two components move in opposite directions, and that only one of them responds to what services contain, is the study's result rather than an intermediate step toward one. Ghana is the empirical setting, but the measurement problem is general to any programme evaluated on aggregate farm performance.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 describes the data, the construction of the community service measures, and the descriptive comparison between served and unserved communities. Section 3 documents agricultural service delivery in Ghana as the surveys record it. Section 4 sets out the meta-stochastic frontier specification, the construction of the matched sample, and what the design does and does not identify. Section 5 reports the results and Section 6 interprets them. Section 7 concludes with the implications for policy and for research design. Supplementary tables and figures are collected in the appendix.
